TRANSLATION. 


First part. 

1. Hail! Prosperity! This (is) the edict (Sdsana) of Rajaraja, (alias) Rajakésari- 
varman, which is cherished by the multitude of the diadems of (i.e., whic is obeyed by) 
the crowd of all princes.? 

2. On the twentieth day of the twenty-sixth year (of the reign) of K6-Rajakésari- 
varman, alias Sri-Rajarajadéva, who,—while (fis) heart rejoiced, that, like thé goddess 
of fortune, the goddess of the great earth had become his wife, —in his life of growing strength, 
_during which, having been pleased to cut the vessel (alam) (im) the hall (af) Kandalfr,® he 
conquered by his army, which was victorious in great battles, Véngai-nadu, Ganga-padi, 
Tadigai-padi, Nulamba-padi, Kudamalai-nédu, Kollam, Kalingam, fra-manda- 
lam, (the conquest of which) gave fame (i.e. made (him) famous) (7) the eight directions, and 
the seven and a half lakshas of Eratia-padi,--deprived the Seriyas (i.e, the Pandyas) 
of their splendour, while (te) was regplendent (f such a degree) that (he) was worthy to bé 
worshipped everywhere ;—having been pleased to make gifts-(é) the royal bathing-hall 
(tiru-maitjana-$dlai) to the east (of the hall) of Irumadi-Soray within the Faiijavar palace 
(kéyil), the lord (udaiydr) Srt-Rajarajadéva vouchsafed to say :—“ Let the gifts made 
by us, those made by (ous) elder sister,* those made by our wives, and those made by other 
donors to the lord (wdaiydr) of the sacred stone-temple (tirukkarrali), (called) Srt-Raja- 
*r4jéSvara,—which we caused to be built (at) Tafijaviy, (a city) in Tafjavar-kdrram, 
(@ subdivision) of PandyakuldSani-valanaédu,—be engraved on stone on the sacred 
shrine (474-vimdna)!” (Accordingly, these gifts) were engraved (as follows) :— 

3. On the three-hundred-and-twelfth day of the twenty-fifth year (of his reign), the 
lord Sri-Rajarajadéva gave one gold (image of) Kolgaidévar,® which is to be present 
(at) the sacred offerings (éré-bali),° weighing eight hundred and twenty-nine karatju” and 

+ three quarters and three maftjddi by the stone called (after) Adavallay.

: No. 2. ON THE WEST WALL. 

This inscription is engraved in five sections, each of which occupies a separate face of 
the west wall. It consists of two distinct parts. 

The first part extends to about two thirds of line 7 of the first section and describes 
eleven gold vessels, which were presented on the 310th day of the 25th year of the reign of 
K6-Rajakésarivarman, alias Rajarajadéva, ‘to (the goddess) Umaparamé$vari, who 
is the consort of our lord Adavallar, by the king’ 8 elder sister,! who was the queen of 
Vallavaraiyar® Vandyadévar. 

The second part enumerates other gifts of gold vessels and ornaments, which were made 
by the same royal lady between the 20th and 29th year of the king’s reign. The items 
detailed in paragraphs I4 to 42 were given ‘to (the goddess) Umaparaméévari, who is 
the consort of our lord Adavallar Dakshina-Méru-Vitankar.’ Paragraphs 44 to 59 
describe gifts ‘to (the goddess) Umaparaméévarti, who is the consort of our lord Tafijai- 
Vitankar.’ : ;

TRANSLATION, 
First part. 


1, Hail! Prosperity ! On the three-hundred-and-tenth day of the twenty-fifth year (of 
the reign) of KO-Rajakésarivarman, alias Sri- Rajarajadéva, who,— while (his) heart 
rejoiced, that, like the goddess of fortune, the goddess of the great earth had become his 
wife,— in his life of growing strength, during which, having been pleased to cut the vessel 
(in) the hall (a#) Kandalfr, he conquered by his army, which was victorious in great 
battles, Véngai-nadu, Ganga-paidi, Tadigai-pidi, Nulamba-p4di, Kudamalai- 
nadu, Kollam, Kalingam, tra-mandalam, (the conquest of which) made (him) famous 
(in) the eight directions, and the seven and a half lakshas of Iratta-p&di,—— deprived the 
Seriyas of their splendour, while (he) was resplendent (to such a degree) that (he) was worthy

No. 8. INSCRIPTION OF RAJARAJA. 21 
No. 3. ON THE NORTH WALL, LOWER TIER. 


This inscription is engraved in 38 sections of 15 lines each and contains a description 
of thirty sacred ornaments. These were made partly of gold and jewels from the temple 
treasury, and partly of pearls, which K6-RAjakésarivarman, alias Rajarajadéva, had 
given to the temple up to the 29th year of his reign. Paragraphs 5 and 6 allude to gold, 
which the king had seized after conquering the Chéra king and the Pandyas, and which 
he had presented to the temple.

TRANSLATION. 


1. Hail! Prosperity! The’ sacred ornaments (dharana) of jewels (raina) of the first 
quality, made (partly) of gold and jewels of the first quality, which had accumulated in the 
treasury (bhandara) of the lord of the Sri-R4jar4jésvara (demple),—excluding those which 
were exhibited (¢o the public ?) at the treasury of the lord of the Sri-Rajar4jésvara 
(temple),—end (partly) of jewels, which the lord Sri-Raj arajadéva had been pleased to 
give (0 the temple) until the twenty-ninth year (of the reign) of K6-Rajakésarivarman, 
aliag Sri-Rajarajadéva, who,—while (fis) heart rejoiced, that, like the goddess of 
fortune, the goddess of the great earth had become his wife,—in his life of growing strength, 
during whicli,, having been’ pleased to cut the vessel (iz) the hall (af) Kandaltr, he 
conquered by his army, which was victorious in great battles, Véngai-nddu, Ganga- 
padi, Tadigai-padi; Nulamba-padi, Kudamalai-nadu, Kollam, Kalingam, fra- 
mandalam, (the conquest of which) made.(him) famous (7m) the eight directions, and the 
seven and a half akshas of Iratta -padi,—deprived the Sefiyas of their splendour, while 
(te) was resplendent (to such a degree) that (he) was worthy to be worshipped every- 
where,—were weighed by the jewel weight (AdSu-kal) called (after) Dakshina-Méru.- 
Vitankan,! excluding-the threads (Saradu) and the frames (Satfam), (but) including the 
lac (arakku) and the pitju, (and) were engraved on stone on the sacred shrine ($rt-vimdna) of 
the lord,—excluding those which had been engraved on stone on the Jjagatippadat and on the 
‘upaptthattu-kandappadat* of the temple (4éyil) of Chand ésvara,—(as follows):— 

2. One sacred girdle (druppattigai), made of gold taken from the treasury of the lord, 
(and containing) ten karatju and three quarters, three mafjddi and (one) kuart of gold, which 
was a quarter inferior in fineness to (the gold standard called) dandavdni. The lac weighed 
eight karafiju and seven mafjddi. The piftju weighed three quarters (of a karafju). Fifteen 
crystals (palingu), set into (ét), weighed (one) karuttju. Tifree potti weighed three mafjddi, 
One thousand five hundred and twelve strung pearls (muttu) of brilliant water and of red 
water, (taken) from the pearls of the second quality, which the lord Sri-Rajara jadéva had 
poured out as flowers at the sacred feet (Sripddapushpa) and with which be had worshipped 
the feet of the god, (vz.) round pearls (vattam), roundish pearls (anuvatiam), polished pearls 
(oppu-muttu), small pearls (kuru-mutiu), nimbolam, payittam, ambumudu, crude pearls (karadu), 
twin pearls (trattat), Sappatti and Sakkattu, weighed forty-one kara%ju and seven maijddi. 
Twenty-four strung corals (pavaram), (taken) from the corals in the treasury, weighed three 
quarters (ofa karafyu), t three mafjddi and (one) kurt. Altogether, {the girdle) weighed sixty- 
three karafju and nine maryadi, corresponding to a value of ninety kdsu. . 

3. One sacred girdle, made of gold taken from the treasury, (and conéaining) ten harattju 
and three quarters and four mafjddi of gold, which: was a quarter inferior in fineness to the 
dandavani, The lac weighed eight ‘arutju and seven matjddi. The pifiju weighed three 
quarters (of a karatju). Fifteen crystals, set into (it), weighed three quarters (of a karanju), 
four manjddi and (one) kugri. Three potti weighed three mafjddi., One thousand five

(#61) and old pearls, weighed twenty-three karafiju and a half, four mafjddi and (one) kunré. 
Altogether, (the parasol) weighed ninety:nine ara%ju and nine maf/ddi, corresponding to a 
value of one hundred and sixty késu. 


No. 4. On tHE sOUTH WALL, SECOND TIER, 

The preserved part of this mscription comprises eight sections of nine lines each. The 
end of each line of the third section, the commencement of each line of the fourth section, 
and the whole of any other section, which may have intervened between the third and 
fourth, are covered by a flight of steps, which was constructed at a period subsequent 

to that, during which the inscription had been iticised. 

The inscription specifies the revenue in paddy and the revenue in gold and in money 
(ku), which a number of villages had to pay to the stone-temple, called Rajarajésvara, 
which Rajardjadéva had caused to be built at Tafijdvar. The villages were situated 
both in the Chéle country and in other countries and had been assigned to the temple by 
Rajarajadéva until the 29th year of his reign. The extent of the land, which the king 
had given to the temple in each of the villages, is recorded in great detail by a land 
measure, the name of which is not stated, and by fractions of it, The paddy due to the 
temple had to be measured by ‘the marakkdl? called (after) Adavallan,’ ie. by a corm 
measure which was preserved at the shrine of the god Adavallan;* and this marakkdl was 
‘equal to a rdjakésari’ This term was evidently derived trom Rajakésarin, the surname of 
the reigning king Rajaraja and of other Chéla kings,* and must be taken as the real name 
of the royal standard measure,’ a copy of which was preserved at the temple. The only 
case, in which the revenue had to be paid in gold, occurs in paragraph 13. No instance of 
payment in money (/déSu) occurs in the preserved part of the inscription,

TRANSLATION. 

1, Hail! Prosperity ! There was engraved on stone, as orally settled, the revenue (kdn'k- 
kadan) in paddy,—which has to be measured by the marakkdl called (after) Adavallan, 
which is equal to a rdjakésari,—and the gold and the money (késu), which have to be paid 
from the land paying taxes; and (there was also engraved on stone) the land free from 
taxes,—including the village-site (sr-nattam), the sacred temples (éri-kéyil), the ponds 
(kulam), the channels (vdykkdl) passing through (the villages), the Paraichchéri,: the Kammdna- 
Séri? and the burning-ground (sudukddu),— in the villages, which the lord Sri-RAjaraja - 
déva had given in the Chéla country (Séra-mandalam) and in other countries as divine 
gifts (dévaddna) for the expenses (nibandha)® required by the supreme lord (paramasvdmin) 
of the sacred stone-temple (tirukkarrali), (called) Sri-Rajarajésvara,—which the lord 
Sri-Rajarajadéva had caused to be built (a¢) Tanjavar,—until the twenty-ninth year 
(of the reign) of K6-Rajakésarivarman, alias Sri-Rajarajadéva, who,—while (his) 
heart rejoiced, that, like the goddess of fortune, the goddess of the great earth had become 
‘his wife,—in his life of growing strength, during which, having been pleased to cut the 
vessel (#z) the hall (at) Kandalar, he conquered by his army, which was victorious in

No. 5. ON. TH# NORTH WALL, UPPER TIER. 


The original of this inscription is divided into two sections of nine lines each. At the 
commencement of each line of the first section, a few syllables are lost, and the first five lines 
of the same section are considerably damaged about the middle. In the first line the date is 
lost. As, however, the preserved part of the historical passage, with which the line opens, 
agrees literally with the corresponding passage of No. 4, the inscription cannot have been 
engraved before the 29th year of the reign of Rajardjadéva. Like No. 4, this inscription 
specifies the revenue in paddy and the revenue in gold, to be paid by a number of villages 
which Rajarajadéva had given to the temple.

No. 6. ON THE SOUTH WALL, SECOND TIER. 


This and the next inscription, though of different date, are engraved continuously ia 
two sections. No. 6 fills the whole of the first section and part of the first line of the 
second section. 

The inscription describes a number of gifts, which were made until the 29th year of 
the reign of K6-Rajakésarivarman, alias Rajarajadéva, by Arvar Parantakap 
Kundavaiy4r, who was the elder sister of Rajaréjadéva and the queen of Vallava- 
raiyar Vandyadévar. As, according to thé large Leyden grant,' Rajaraéja was the son 
of Parantaka II., it is evident that the name of his sister, Pardntekay Kundavaiydr, is an 
abbreviation for Pardntakan magal Kundavaiydry i.e. Kundavaiy4r, the daughter of 
Parantaka (II). 

Paragraph 2 records a gift of gold to the same two goddesses, who are mentioned in the 
inscription No. 2.2 According to paragraph 1, these two images had been set up in 
the temple of RajarajéSvara by Kundavaiy4r herself. The same prineess had set up 
an image of her mother, to which she presented certain ornaments (paragraphs 3 to 5). 
Other ornaments were given to the image of the god Dakshina-Méru-Vitankar (para- 
graphs 6 and 7), which had been set up by king Rajardjadéva (paragraph 1), and to his 
consort (paragraphs 8 and 9), who was one of the two goddesses referred to in paragraph 2. 
The remainder of the inscription treats of endowments to these two goddesses (paragraph 
10), to the image of Ponmaligaittufijiga-dévar (paragraph 14), and to the image of the 
mother of Kundavaiy4r (paragraph 19), These endowments were made in the following 
manner. Kundavaiyar deposited certain sums of money (4dsu), which were subsequently 
borrowed on interest by the inhabitants of certain villages from the shrine of Chandésvara 
(paragraph 1), the saint in whose name the money affairs of temples are generally trans- 
acted.’ The interest had to be paid yearly into the treasury of the RajarajéSvara temple at 
Tafijavdr either in paddy‘ or in money. In the former case, the interest was three kuruni 
of paddy for each Aééu, and in the latter 123 per cent. If it is assumed that the rate 
of interest was the same in both cases, one kd$u would correspond to the value of 24 kurunt 
or 2 kalam of paddy. In two instances (paragraphs 18 and 21), money was deposited for 
purchasing a number of sheep, from the milk of which two private individuals had to supply 
daily a certain amount of ghee for lamps.’ ‘The value of one sheep was reckoned as 3 kdsu. 
In paragraphs 14 and 19, the value of various daily requirements is given in measures 
of paddy ; the whole list probably represents the daily wants of a single pujdrt.

No. 8. ON THE WALLS OF THE, PORTICO, SECOND TIER. 


This inscription is engraved on the south, east and north walls of a portico, which forms 
the main entrance on the east of the central shrine.” The published text, which consists of 
three sections of nine lines each, efids in the middle of paragraph 26 with the statement, 
that the inscription is continued at the bottorg of the south wall of the portico, Of this 
portion mo copy could be taken, as the present pavement of the temple court rises to its level. 

Like the preceding inscription, this one describes a number of ornaments of gold and . 
jewels, which were presented by Arvar Parantakay Kundavaiy4r until the 3rd year of 
the reign of Ké6-Parakésarivarman, alias Raéjéndra-Chéladéva. The donees were 
the images which she had set up herself. Among these, the published part of the inscrip- 
tion mentions the consort of Dakshina-»Méru-Vitankar (paragraph 2) and the consort , 
of Tafijai- Vitankar (paragraphs 8 and 24). ;

No. 9 is dated in the 6th year of the reign of Ké6-Parakésarivarman, dias

No. 20. ON THE SOUTH WALL, FIRST AND SECOND TIERS. 


This inscription records that, on the 242nd day of the 19th year of his reign, Rajén- 
dra-Chéladéva granted a yearly allowance of paddy to a Saiva priest of the Rajarajés-_ 
vara temple. He issued this order from his palace at Gangaikonda-Sérapuram.® 

* The most important part of the inscription is the end of its historical introduction, 
which adds a number of names of places, which the king had conquered between his 12th 
and 19th year, to those mentioned in two Tirumalai inscriptions of the 12th year.* 
Among these additional names of localities I can identify none but the last, viz, Kadaram 


1 The historical part of this inscription is identical with that of No. 10. 

2 This place is situated in the Udaiydrpalaiyam talluga of the Trichinopoly district; see Mr. Sewell’s 
Lists of Antiquities, Vol. I, p. 264. 

3 Vol. I, Nos. 67 and 68. 


106 INSCRIPTIONS ON THE CENTRAL SHRINE. 


(line 11), whose king, called Samgrdmavijayéttungavarman, was attacked by sca 
and caught (IL 8 f.). This: king must have been a successor of Maravijayéttunga- 
varman, the son of Chiddmanivarman and king of Kataha or Kidéram, who is 
mentioned in the large Leyden grant! as a vassal of Rajaraja, Kidaram is now the 
head-quarters of a talluga of the Ramnfid Zamindart in the Madura district.* The remain- 
ing names of localities, which I am unable to identify,.must probably be looked for in the 
same neighbourhood, as the inscription seems to imply that they were all taken from the king 
of Kadiram, together with Kadaram itself, which is the last item in the list, 

At the beginning of each line of the second tier of this inscription, a few letters are lost. 
Most of these can be supplied with certainty from other inscriptions of Rajéndra-Chéla, 
Those letters which are lost at the beginning of lines @ to 11, are taken from an undated 
inscription of the Kailésandtha temple at Uttaramallirs The Bilvandthésvara 
temple at Tiruvallam contains inscriptions of the 21st, 26th and ([3]1st years of Rajén-~ 
dra-Chéla.* Owing to their imperfect preservation, these were of very little use for the 
restoration of the text. As the historical passage at their beginning adds nothing new to 
that of the subjoined inscription, they serve at least to prove, that Rajéndra-Chéla did 
not make any further conquests after the 19th year of his reign. ~

fifth year’ of Tribhuvanachakravartin Kénéripmai-kondan. As I have shown in 
a paper on the Tirunelli deed of Bhaskara Ravivarman, which will shortly appear in the

Indian Antiquary, the word ‘ opposite’ (edi) is used in Tamil dates ih the sense of ‘after.’ 
Accordingly, this inscription is dated in the year which followed after the fifth year, z.¢., in 
the sixth year of the king’s reign. The name of the king has remained a puzzle and has 
been misread in various ways, until my assistant discovered an archaic inscription at. 
Kuttalam near Mayavaram, in which it is spelt Qs1@erQ@earenn@srertrer, This spell- 
ing,—if compared with the usual forms, Qsr@eferanwGeréerrer and GarQer fen anw- 
@arsnrtrer,—shows that the first part of the name must be divided into @a1@a#-+ @arenw., 
From the assimilated form @a«@sfienw, which occurs in an inscription at Pallavaram,! 
we may further conclude that Qerenn is meant for @strenw. @ar@er must be dissolved 
into Gar, ‘a king,’ and Gaz, ‘ equality,’ and @srenw is an abstract of the root @e, which 
signifies negation. Ké-nér-il-mai-konddy may thus be translated by ‘he who ‘has assumed 
the title “the unequalled among kings ”’ and is synonymous with Kégénmai-konddn, ‘he 
who has assumed the title “king of kings,’ a surname of the Chéra king Bhaskara 
Ravivarman, to whose reign the Cochin deed of the Jews* belongs. Kénéril or Konéril 
appears to have been corrupted subsequently into Kénéri. For, we find-the surname 
Kénéri-mél-kondan or Konéri-mén-konda applied to Vira-Chéla and to Kulét- 
tunga-Chéladéva ;* and on a coin,* copies of which are not rarely met with at Tanjore 
and Madura, the legend is Qer@erflrrwetr, K6néri-rayan. 

The title Kénériimai-kondén is applied to the Chéla king Rajarfjadéva in the 
large Leyden grant (line 112); to Kul6ttunga-Chéladéva in an inscription at Karuvar;° 
and to Sundara-Pandya in an inscription of the Madura temple,’ in the cave-inscription 
at Tirupparankuyram,’ in the smaller Tiruppivanam grant,® and in inscriptions at 
Pérfr.® The same surname was borne by Vira-Pandya and by Kulasékharadéva.¥ 
The king to whose reign the present, inscription belongs, must be different from, and con- 
siderably later than, R&ajarajadéva, whose inscriptions are written in archaic charace 
ters, while those of the subjoined inscription are not very far removed from the modern 
Tamil ones. There is no such objection to identifying the Kénériymai-kondan of the 
subjoined inscription with one of the three Pandya kings, who had-that surname. But it 
is impossible to make any final identification, as the inscription does not contain any 
historical particulars about the king to whose reign it, belongs. 

The inscription records an order of the king, by which certain lands, that had been 
wrongfully sold during the third and fourth years of his reign, were restored to the temple’ 
of Rajaraja-[évara at Tafijavar.

No. 22. INSCRIPTION OF KONERINMAI-KONDAN. 113 


western extremity of the city of Tafijavar. The village was divided into 108 shares, of 
which 106 were to be enjoyed by the Brihmanas of the village of Simantanfrayana- 
chaturvédimangalam near Tafijavér, and 2 by the temple of Samantand@rayana- 
Vinnagar-Emberum4n in this village. Both this villageand this temple had been called 
after his own name, and the granted village had been purchased from its former owners, by a 
person, who is designated in the text as the TondaimAnar, but whose proper name must 
accordingly have been Simantandrayana. He was apparently a feudatory or high officer 
of the king, who made the grant at his instance and on his behalf. At the present time the 
title of Tondaim4n is borne by the chiefs of the state of Pudukk6ttai in the Trichinopoly 
district. Their ancestor is reported to have ousted one Pallavarayan Tondaimay about 
1680 A.D.' This chief was probably a descendant of Simantanardyana Tondaim4én 
and of Karunfkara Tondaim4n, who, according to the Tamil poem Kalingattu-Parani,* 
was king of the Pallavas, resided at Vandai* and was the prime minister of the Chéla king 
Kuléttunga. The title Tondaim4n means the king of Tondai* or Tondaimandalam, 
the Tamil name of the Pallava country, the ancient capital of whjch was Kafichipuram. 
The numerous Chéla inscriptions found at this town prove that the Pallava kingdom must 
have fallen a prey to the Chélas. From the Kuliigatiu-Parani it further appears, that the 
former rulers of Tondaimandalam were allowed to retain possession of their dominions as 
feudatories. In the subjoined inscription they appear in the same position during the time of 
Kénérinmai-kondan. ‘ 
The chief difficulty in this inscription are the numerous fiscal terms mentioned in 
. connection with the grant. A good many of them had to be left untranslated,® while the 
translation of others is only tentative.

No. 23. On THE SOUTH WALL, FIRST TIER. 


This inscription contains an order of ‘king Tirumalaidéva, by which a number of 
villages were exempted from taxes. This was probably done, because they had been granted 
to the Tafijavdr temple. The date of the inscription is Saka 1377 (expired), the cyclic year 
Yuvan, t.c., A.D. 1455. Consequently, the king to whose reign it belongs, must be distinct 
from the Karnata king Tirumalaidéva, whose four inscriptions near Vélfr are dated in 
Saka 1488 (expired).* It is not impossible that Tirumalaidéva is identical with Timma, the 
founder of the second dynasty of Vijayanagara, for whose grandson Narasa, Nrisimba 
or Narasitmha we have the dates Saka 1404 and 1418.° In favour of this identification it can be 
adduced, that in the subjoined inscription, Tirumalaidéva receives the same dirudas which 
were borne by Narasimhadéva according to an inscription at Virifichipuram,” and

No. 24. In THE INNER GOPURA, ON THE LEFT OF THE ENTRANCE. 


This inscription is dated in the 29th year of the reign of K4-Rajakésarivarman, alias 
Rajarijadéva, and opens with the same historical passage as Nos. 1 to 3.1 “It records two 
deposits of money, which were made by an officer of king Rajara4jadéva in favour of the 
chief idol of the Rajar4jésvara temple, and of the image of Dakshina-Méru-Vitankar. 
The first deposit was lent to the inhabitants of a ddzdr at Tafijavar, who had in exchange 
to supply cardamom seeds and champaka buds, and the second deposit to certain villagers, 
who had to supply Ahaskhas roots. These three kinds of drugs were used for scenting the 
bathing-water of the two gods.

mandalam, (the conquest of which) made (him) famous (én) the eight directions, and the

for khaskhas (roots), to be thrown into the bathing-water and on the surface of the fresh

by using ‘ the interest.

No, 24. It records two deposits of money, which were made by a manager of the Rajara-

which is as detailed as, and still more extensive than, the one given in the inscription No. 6, 
paragraphs 14 and 19. The interest of the second deposit,was to be paid in money and to 
be used for purchasing camphor, which had to be burnt before the images of Rajarajés- 
vara and Dakshina-Méru-Vitankar,

No. 28. IN THE INNER GOPURA, ON THE: RIGHT OF THE ENTRANCE. 


This inscription is engraved underneath the preceding No. 27. It is considerably 
injured, especially in the first ten lines. The date is only partially preserved, but, to judge 
from paragraph 6, was the same as that of No. 27. The inscription records a deposit of 
money, the interest of which was to be used for feeding ten Siva-yégins on each of twenty-four 
festival days. The name of the donor is lost.

No, 29. ON a PILLAR OF THE EAST ENCLOSURE, TO THE RIGHT OF THE GoPURA,! 


This inscription describes a number of copper images, which king Rajaradjadéva had 
set up in the Rajarajésvara temple before the 29th year of his reign. These images were 
probably arranged in two groups, which represented two successive scenes from the life of the 
Saiva saint Chandés vara, as described in the Periyapurdnam.* The first group may have 
consisted of a linga (Mah4déva, paragraph 8), of a statue of Chand ésvara who worshipped 
it (paragraph 10), and of one of his father,* who was killed by his own son, because he 
obstructed the worship of Siva (paragraph 11). The second group was probably composed 
of Siva and his consort (paragraphs 2 and 5), and of ChandéSvara (paragraph 12), who 
received a flower-garland from Siva as a reward for his devotion (paragraph 18).

1 On similar surnames see p. 125, note 2. In the large Leyden grant, the same surname of Krishna 
Rama occurs twice (lines 131 and 163), while he is called Rajéndra-Séra-brahma-m[4*]rayan at the end of that 
inscription (line 437,f.). In the first two instances, he is designated as chief secretary (élat-ndyakan) of Raja-

1890, G.O., dated 11th March 1890, No. 189, Public) had the surname Mummudi-Séradéva. Consequently, the 
first surname of Krishna Rama means ‘the great king of the Brahmans of Mummadi-Chéla, ¢.6., Mummudi- 
Chéla or Rajaraja.’ The third occasion, on which Krishna Rima’s name occurs in the Leyden grant, shows 
that, after the accession of Rajéndra-Chéla, who issued the grant after the death of his father Rajaraja, the 
original sirname was changed into ‘the great king of the Brahmanes of Rajéndra-Chélag This change is 
an additional proof of the identity of Rajéndra-Chéla with Madhurantaka (Vol. I, p. 96).

No. 34. On a NICHE AND A PILLAR OF THE SOUTH ENCLOSURE, 


This inscription records that Lékamah4dévit, a queenof Rajardjadéva, set up a 


copper image of Pichchadévar, to which she presented a number of ornaments 
(paragraphs 9 to 19) and two vessels of gold and silver (paragraphs 20 and 21). The image

mentioned in the present inscription,—a goblin (Bia), an antelope and a skull (paragraphs 
3, 5 and 21),—it may be concluded that the image was one of Siva?

No. 38. ON THE FIRST NICHE OF THE WEST ENCLOSURE, THIRD INSCRIPTION. 


This inscription describes seven images, which had been set up before the 29th year [of 
the reign of Rajarajadéva] by the same manager of the Rajarajésvara temple, who is 
mentioned in the inscription No. 26, and a number of ornaments, which had been given to 
these images by the same person (paragraphs 23 to 50) and by the inhabitants of two 
towns (paragraphs 51 and 59). The,images represented Nambi-Ardrandar (paragraphs 2, 
23, 55, 59), Nangai-Paravaiydar (5, 25, 57, 66), Tirundvukkaraiyar (8, 29, 53), 
Tirufldnasgambandadigal (11, 36, 61), Periya-Perumal (14, 44), his consort 
Lékamahadévi (17, 47), and the god Chandrasékhara® (20). Of these, Periya- 
Perumal, ‘the great king,’ and his consort Lékamahadévt are perhaps identical with 
king RAjarajadéva and his queen Lékamah&dévi,* both of whom may have been 
represented as worshipping the god Chandrasékhara, 2.e., Siva, in whose honour the king 
had built the temple. . 

The inscription is of great importance for the history of Tamil literature, as it forms a 
terminus ad quem for the time of the reputed authors of the Dévdram or Miivar-pddal, a 
collection of hymns in honour of Siva. Dr. Caldwell‘ was inclined to assign this poem to the 
end of the thirteenth century. But the present inscription shows, that it must have been 
written before the time of Rajardéjadéva. For the inscription mentions each of the three 
authors of the Dévdram, viz.. Tirufidpasambandar, Tirunavukkaraiyar (alas Appar) 
and Nambi-Ardran4r (alias Sundaramérti), also the latter’s wife Nangai-Paravaiyar. 

It is not improbable, that the sixty-three Tiruttondar or Saiva devotees, among 
whom the three authors of the Dévdram are reckoned, belong to a much earlier period 
than that of Rajardjadéva. For one of them, who is mentioned along with the rest in 
Sundaramirti’s hymns,* was Kéchchengannady,® the son of the Chéla king 
Subhadéva and of his queen Kamalavati.’ This Kichchengann4n appears to be identical 
with the Chéla king Sengan, the hero of Poygaiy4r’s contemporaneous Tamil poem 
Kalavari, which was recently translated by Mr. V. Kanakasabhai Pillai.* The same scholar

No. 40. On two PILLARS OF THE WEST ENCLOSURE. 


This short inscription is dated in the 3rd year of the reign of R4j éndra-Chéladéva 
and records the setting-up of a copper image by the same manager of the Rajarajésvara 
temple, whose name we have found in two inscriptions of the 29th year of the reign of 


* Q5GGA or OFSGSHAA, vulga OpiigsG, is a kind of thistle, Tribulus terrestris, L. (Winslow). 


No. 40. INSCRIPTION OF RAJENDRA-CHOLA. 167 


Rijarajadéva.' Itcommands considerable interest, because it refers explicitly to the legend 
of one of the Tiruttondar, as preserved in the Periyapurdnam.* In the 6th chapter of this 
book, we are told how Meypporunayanar, a Chédi(!) king residing at Tirukkéva- 
lair,® was stabbed by his enemy Muttanddan, who had managed to obtain a private 
interview in the disguise of a Saiva devotee. The door-keeper Tattan, who intended to kill 
the murderer, was prevented by the dying king, who exclaimed:—“ Oh Tattan! he is 
a devotee of Siva; therefore do not harm him !_or, as expressed in the verse which is 
“prefixed to the story:—“(He 7s) one of us, oh Tattan!” In the subjoined inscription, 
the corresponding words are:—“Oh Tattan! (he 8) one of us; see!”—* and the person 
who utters them, is calléd Milad-udaiy4r, ‘the lord of Milddu.’ This designation of 
Meypporunayanar is synonymous with Maldda-mannar, ‘the king of the inhabitants of 
Malidu,’* in the opening verse, and with Malaiya-mdndtidrukku arasar, ‘the king of the 
inhabitants of the great country-of hills,’ in the prose version. 

In the introduction to No. 38, it was mentioned that Sékkirar, the author of the 
original poetical version of the Periyapurdnam, wrote during the reign of the Ch6] a king 
Anapaya, alias Kuléttunga-Chéladéva. The characters of the Tiruvarir inscription 
of this prince are decidedly more modern than those of the Tafijavar inscriptions of 
Rajaraja and Rajéndra-Ch6éla. Accordingly, the Periyapurdnam must have been 
composed after their time. On the other hand, the subjoined inscription proves that the 
legends, which Sékkirar embodied in his work, were not of his own invention, but must 
have grown up in the time of the predecessors of Rajéndra-Chéla.

TRANSLATION. 


1. Hail! Prosperity ! The following copper images,—which had been set up in the 
temple of the lord Srt- Rajarajésvara until the twenty-ninth year (of the king’s reign) 
by Séramahadéviyar, the consort of our lord Srt- Rajardjadéva,—were engraved 
on stone, after they had been measured by the cubit measure (preserved) in the temple 
of the lord, after the jewels (given to them) had been weighed without the threads, the 
frames and the copper nails by the stone called (after) Dakshina-Méru-Vitankan, and 
after the gold had been weighed by the stone called (after) A dawallan :— 

2. One solid image of Adavallar, having four divine arms, (the goddess) Ganga- 
bhattdraki on the braided hair, nine braids of hair (jatd) and seven flower-garlands 
(piimdlai), and (measuring), together with (an image of) MuSalagay who was lying on 
the ground, three quarters and one eighth of a muram in height from the feet to the hair. 

3. One lotus on which this (image) stood, set with jewels and measuring three viral 
in height. 

4. One pedestal, measuring five viral in height, half a muram in length, and ten viral 
in breadth. 

5. One solid aurcola (measuring), three muram and two viral in circumference. 

6. One solid image of his consort UmAparaméSvari, measuring seventeen viral and 
two ¢érad in height from the feet to the hair. 

7. One lotus on which this (image) stood, set with jewels and measuring two viral and 
two térai in height.

No. 43. ON THB BASE OF THE WEST ENCLOSURE. 

The date of this inscription and the name of the donor are only partially preserved, 
but were doubtlessly the same as in the inscriptions Nos. 40 and 41. It records the setting- 
up of copper images of two gods,—K shétrapaladéva (paragraph 2) and Bhairava (7),— 
and of three human beings, who were arranged in a group (24). These were Siruttonda- 
Nambi (12), (his wife) Tiruvenkattu-Nangai (16) and (their son) Siraladévar (19), 
who, according to the Periyapurdnam,? was killed by his parents and served up as a meal to 
Siva in his form of Bhairava. Thus the inscription is an additional proof of the antiquity 
of the legends, which are embodied in the Periyapurdnam, and some of which are referred to 
in other inscriptions of Rajaraja (No. 38) and Rajéndra-Chéla (Nos. 40 and 41). 
Siruttondan is already mentioned in the Dévdram of Tirufidpasambandar.

No. 44. ON a PILLAR OF THE WEST ENCLOSURE. 


This inscription records that, before the 29th year of the reign of Rajardjadéva, his 
queen Abhimanavalli set up @ copper image, the name of which is only partially pre- 
served. It seems however that it was a liiga (paragraph 2) and that images of Siva (3), 
Brahman (4), and Vishnu in his boar-incarnation (5) attended it. 

The whole group probably referred to the following legend, which is narrated in the 
Arundchala-Mdhdtmya, a mythical account of the Saiva temple at Tiruvannamalai in the 
South Arcot district:—“Siva appeared as a fiery liaga to Brahman and Vishnu, and 


No. 44. INSCRIPTION OF RAJARAJA. 175 


desired them to seek his base and summit, which they attempted in vain.”' On this occa- 
sion, Vishnu is said to have assumed the shape of a boar,’ as stated in the subjoined 
inscription. ;

No. 46. ON TWo NICHES AND TWO PILLARS OF THE WEST ENCLOSURE. - 


This inscription commences on the same niche as the preceding No. 45, is continued 
on the four faces of each of two pillars, and ends on another niche. It records that, before 
the 29th year of the reign of Rajardjadéva, his queen Chélamahadévt set up copper 
images of Rishabhavahanadéva, #.e., Siva whose vehicle is the bull, of his consort Uma- 
paramésvari, and of their son Ganapati, and that she presented various ornaments to 
each of these three images.

- TRANSLATION, 


J. Hail! Prosperity! The following copper images,—which had been set up in the 
temple of the lord Sri-Rajarajésvara until the twenty-ninth year (of the king’s reign) by 
Ssramahadéviy ar, the consort of our lord Sri-Rajarajadéva,—were engraved on stone, 
after they had been measured by the cubit measure (preserved) in the temple of ‘the lord, 
after the jewels (given to them) had been weighed without the threads, the frames and the 
copper nails by the stone called (after) Dakshina-Méru-Vitankan, and after the gold and 
silver had been weighed by the stone called (after) Adavallan:— 

2. One solid image of Rishabhavahanadéva, having four divine arms and (measur- 
ing) one muyam, ten viral and two ¢érai in height from the feet to the hair. 

3. One lotus on which this (image) stood, set with jewels and measuring three viral 
and a half in height. 

4, One solid image of his consort UmAparaméévart, measuring one muram and. five 
viral in height from the feet to the hair. 

5. One lotus on which this (cmage) stood, set with jewels and measuring two viral and a 
half in height. 

6. One bull (rishabha), (partially) solid (and partially) hollow, and measuring one muram, 
six viral and five dérai in height from the hoofs to the horns. 

‘7. One pedestal on which the god, his consort and the bull stood, (usiaussig) two 
muram, one viral and two ¢érad in length, one and a quarter muram in breadth, and ten viral 
and one ¢érai in height, and having on its two sides (nerri) two lions (sinha), which jutted 
out five viral and six térai (and measured) four viral and a half in breadth, and eight viral 
and a half in height. 

8.. One solid aureola, covering the ‘god, his consort and the bull, consisting of two 
pillars and one half-moon,’ and measuring six muram, nine viral and a half in circum. 
ference. 

9. One solid image of Ganepeth measuring half a muram and five dérai in height from 
the feet to the ‘hair. 

10. One lotus on which (this image) stood, set with jewels and measuring two viral and 
‘a half in height. 

11. One pedestal, measuring nine viral in length, eight viral in breadth, and four viral 
and two éérai in height. | 

12. One solid aurecla, measuring one (muram) and three quarters and five viral in cir- 
cumference. 

13. To (the image of) Rishabhavahanadéva were given :— 

14. One small sacred garland (¢iru-médlaz), weighing, with the lac, six karafju and a half, 
four mafijédi and (one) kunri, and worth eleven kdsu. On (éf) were fastened fifty-six crystals, 
twenty-four potti and thirty-six pearls, viz., polished pearls and small pearls, 

15. One tutturu, weighing, with the lac, (one) sarafju and a half, three maftjddi and 
eight tenths, and worth three kdSu. On (/#) were fastened one crystal and twenty-two 
pearls, viz., round pearls, roundish pearls, polished pearls and small pearls. 

16. One string (vadam), weighing, with the lac, three Aaruiju and three quarters,, three 
mafjadi and three tenths, and worth sixteen /dsu. On (ct) were strung thirty-three pearls,— 
viz, round pearls, roundish pearls, polished pearls, small pearls, zimbolam, (pearls) with

and eight tenths, and worth fifteen /dsu. On (7/) were strung thirty-five pearls,—v:z., round

No. 47. ON a PILLAR OF THE WEST ENCLOSURE. 


This inscription records that, before the 29th year of the reign of Rajardjadéva, 
an officer of the king set up a copper image of Bhringisa, to which he presented some 
ornaments. 

Regarding Bhringi, Iam indebted for the following information to Mr. P. Sundaram 
Pillai, M.A., Professor of Philosophy, Trivandrum College :— “Bhringi is one of the 
attendants (gana) of Siva, Allusions to his bigoted worship of Siva, which would not con- 
descend even to acknowledge the godhead of Parvati, are frequent in Tamil literature, 


No. 47. INSCRIPTION OF RAJARAJA. 191 


According to the Shéndapurdnam, it was to annoy his exclusive spirit, that Parvati sought 
union with Siva in the form of Ardhanfrigévara. But Bhriigi assumed the shape of a bee! 
and pierced his way through the united body of the god and the goddess, going round and 
worshipping the Siva portion only of the hermaphrodite, The goddess avenged herself then 
by withdrawing all Sak¢i from the zealot, and he is now generally represented as a skeleton, 
supporting himself with a third leg, which Siva, out of mercy, improvised for him.” In accord- 
ance with this myth, three legs and three arms are attributed to the image of Bhringisa in 
paragraph 2 of the subjoined inscription.

No. 51. INSCRIPTION OF RAJARAJA. 203 


No. 51. On rwo NicHES AND TWO.PILLARS OF THE NORTH "ENCLOSURE. 


This inscription records that, before the 29th year of the reign of Raj ara jadéva, his 
queen Pafichavan-mahadévi (paragraphs 1, 36 and 37) set up copper images of Siva called 
Taifijaiyaragar, of his wife UmaparaméS$vari, and of their son Ganapati, to which 
she presented a number of valuable ornaments. The description of some of these ornaments 
is still more detailed than usual, and often obscure, because the meanings of part of the 
technical terms are unknown. As regards the name of the chief image, its first part, 
Taifijai,' is the same as Tafijai or Tafijdvar. The second part, Aragar, means ‘the 
beautiful one.’ The whole name would thus be synonymous with that of the god Tafijai- 
Vitankar, who must, however, be distinct from Taifijaiyaragar, as the image of his consort 
had been set up by Kundavaiy ar, the elder sister of Rajarajadéva.%

1. Hail! Prosperity ! The foHowing copper images,—which had been set up in the 


temple of the lord Sri-Ra jaréjéSvara until the twenty-ninth year (of the king’s reign) by 

Pafichavan-mah4dévi, the consort of our lord Sri-Rajarajadéva,—were engraved on 

stone, after they had been measured by the cubit measure (preserved) in the temple of the lord, 

after the jewels (given to them) had been weighed by the stone called (after) Dakshina- 

Méru-Vitankan, and after the gold and silver- had been weighed by the stone called 
(after) Adavallan —

arms and (measuring) two muram and four viral in height from the feet to the hair,— 
including (an image of) MuSéalagan, who was lying under that sacred foot, on which (the 
god) stood.?

No. 57. ON THE OUTSIDE OF THE EAST ENCLOSURE. 


This inscription is engraved on the left of the entrance to the second gépura,® the inside 
of which bears the inscriptions Nos. 24 to 28. Paragraph 1 states, that it is the continua- 
tion of another inscription, now much obliterated, to the north of “ the gate of Rajaraja,” 
t.e., to the right of the second gépura. As the preserved portion of the inscription is not 
dated, it remains doubtful if it has to be assigned to the reign of Rajarajadéva or to that 
of Rajéndra-Chéladéva. It consists of a list of villages, which had to supply watchmen for 
the temple.

The king, to whose reign these inscriptions belong, is identical with the hero .of the 
. Kalingattu-Parani, a historical poem in Tamil, extracts from which were published by Mr. - 
Kanakasabhai.* This identity may be safely concluded from the mention of the following 
particulars hoth in the inscriptions and in the poem:—l. The conquest of Chakrakétta 
by Kuléttunga, while he was still a Yuvardja.* 2. The battle at Manalfr® on the ‘Tun 
gabhadra.® 3. The defeat of the five Pandyas.’ 4. The conquest of Kéttaru.* 
5. The conquest of Kalinga.® 6. The name of one of Kuléttuiga’s queens, TyAgavallt.» 
7. His surname Jayadhara."” ° ¥ ‘ 
According to the Kaliigaittu-Parani, Kul6ottuiga’s father belonged to the lunar race, and 
his mother was the daughter of Rajaraja or Gangaikonda-Chéla of the solar race." As 
pointed out by Mr. Kanakasabhai ‘and Dr. Fleet, * it follows from these statements, that the 
hero of the poem is identical with the Eastern Chalukya king Kuldttunga-ChédadévaL., 
who reigned from A.D. 1063 to 1112; that his unnamed father and mother were the 
Eastern Chalukya king Rajaraja I.“ and Ammangadévt; and that his maternal grand- 
father,—though inaccurately called Rajaraja in the text of the ppem,—was the Chéla king 
Rajéndra-Chéladéva or Gangaikonda-Chéla. ‘A’ few important details regarding 
the reign of Kuldttunga I. are recorded in the Chellfr grant of Vira-Chéda.“ He was 
originally called R&jéndra-Chéda,—evidently after his maternal grandfather, the Chéla 
king Rajéndra-Chéla,—and ruled over the country of Véngi. Having conquered Kérala, © 
Pandya and Kuntala (the country of the Western Chalukyas), he ‘ascended the throne of 
the Chéla kingdom under the name Kuldttungadéva. By his queen Madhurantaki, the 
daughter of the Chéla king Rajéndradéva, he had seven sons. His original dominion, 
the country of Véngi, he governed through viceroys, viz., 1. his-paternal uncle Vijay 4-

ditya VII. (A.D, 1063 to 1077); 2. his son R&jaraja UL. (A.D. 1077 to 1078); and 3 3.

SéméSvara II. and the coronation of the latter’s younger brother Vikramaditya VI. in 
A.D. 1076, According to the Vikramdnkachurita, Rajiga was the ally of SéméSvara IT. and 
was put to flight by Vikramaditya VI. while Sémésvara II. was taken prisoner.4 Those who 
know the habits of Indian court-poets; will not be surprised to find, that the inscriptions of 
Kul6ttunga differ from the Vikramdikacharita by claiming the victory for the Chélas. In 
the subjoined inscription (ll. 23 ff.) Vikkalan, «e., Vikramaditya VI., is said to have fled 
before Kuldttunga from Nangili (in Maisfr) to the Tungabhadra river, which appears to 
‘have then formed the southern limit of the Western Chalukya dominions. The smaller 
Leyden grant and a few similar inscriptions of Kul6ttunga couple, the name of Vikkalan with 
that of Singanan, #e., Jayasithha IV. whom his elder brother Vikramaditya VI. appointed 
viceroy of Banavase.> As the Vikraménkacharita places Rajiga’s usurpation of the Chéla 
throne shortly before A.D. 1076, it follows that the reign of 49 years from A.D. 1063 to 
1112, which one of the Eastern Chalukya grants ° attributes to Kuléttunga, must include the 
time during which he was only heir-apparent of the Chéla kingdom. ‘he name of his pre- 
decessor on the Chéla throne is not mentioned in the two chronicles. The Vitramdakacharita 
relates that, before Rijiga usurped the Chéla throne, Vikramaditya VI. married the 
daughter of the then Chéla king, and that after the latter’s death he secured the throne to 
his wife’s brother, who shortly after lost his life.’ The Kalitgattu-Parani (x. 26) calls 
Kuldttunga’s predecessor * the king of kings” (mazzar mannavag). The eighth canto of the 
same poem contains 4 short summary of the history of the Chdélas. The last verse (30) of 
this poetical history probably refers to -the reign of Kuléttunga, and the preceding verse 
. (29), which speaks of a king who defeated. the Kuntalas (¢.e., the Western Chalukyas) at 
Kidal-sam gama, to Kuldttunga’s predecessor on the throne. The battle at Kidal-sam-

No. 59. ON THE EAST, NORTH AND WEST WALLS: OF THE CHANDESVARA SHRINE. 


This and the next inscription (No. 60) are engraved on the’ walls of the small shrine 
of Chandéévara, which is situated opposite to the North entrance of the central shrine of 
‘Rajarajésvara. No. 59 describes one diadem and nine girdles for the use of the image of 
Rajarajésvara, the chief idol of the temple. These ornaments were made partly of gold 
and jewels from the temple treasury, and partly ef pearls, which king Rajarajadéva had 
presented to the temple before the 29th year of his reign. A number of corals, which 
formed part of the ornaments, were purchased by the temple treasurers for gold, Which the 
king had seized after conquering the Chéra king and the Pandyas® (paragraphs 2, 3, 4, 9 
and 11) in Malainddu® (paragraph 3). . 

This inscription is referred to as being engraved on the walls of the temple of Chan- 
désvara in paragraph 1 of the inscription No. 3, which is a mere continuation of the 
present inscription.

TRANSLATION. 


1. Hail! Prosperity ! [The sacred ornaments] of jewels of the first quality, made 
(partly) of [gold] and jewels [of the first quality, which had accumulated] in the treasury [of 
the lord of the Sri-RAjar4jéévara (femple)],—excluding those which [were exhibited (to 
the public?) at the treasury of the lord of the Sri-RAjar]4jésvara (temple),—and (partly) 
of jewels, which the lord Sri-Rajara jadéva had been pleased to give (¢o the temple) [until 
the twenty-ninth year (of che reign) of] K6-Rajakésarivarman, alias [Sri-Rajaraja- 
déva], who,—while (Ais) heart rejoiced, that, like the goddess of fortune, the goddess of the 
great earth had become his wife,—in his life of growing strength, during which, having 
been pleased to destroy the ships (a) Kandalfr-Salai,’ he conquered by his army, 
which was victorious in great battles, Véngai-nédu, Ganga-padi, Tadigai-padi, 
Nulamba-padi, Kudamalai-nadu, (Kollam, Kalingam], fra-mandalam, (the 
conquest of which) made (him) famous (in) the eight directions, and the seven and a half dakshas 
of Iratta-padi,—deprived the Seriyas of their splendour, while (4e) was resplendent (to 
such a degree) that (he) was worthy to be worshipped everywhere,—[were weighed by the 
jewel weight called (affer) Dakshina-Méru-Vitankay, exclusive of the threads and of 
the frames, (Ju¢) inclusive of the lac and of the pi%ju, and were engraved on stone] (as 
Sollows) :— : 


' That this is the correct translation of the ambiguous words ers seqtéertas san ms sah, may be 
concluded from two inscriptions of the Chéla king Ké-Rajekésarivarman, alvas Rajadhirajadéva, at Vélir and 
Tiruppangili, which read:— Oeraer OalmQagp erisenterta sonminIsgH; ‘“ (he) caused to be 
destroyed the ships (of) Séralan (#.¢., the Chéra king) (at) Kandaltr-Salai, which is situated on the sea.’’ 
Accordingly, Kandalir-Salai appears to be a place on the Malabar coast. In the Kolingattu-Parans (xi. 71) 
the ehortor form Salai is used for it.

No. 61. ON THE WEST WALL oF THE BRIHANNAYAKI SHRINE. 
e 


This and the next inscription (No. 62) are engraved on the west wall of a shrine, which 
is situated on the north side of the large Nandi.’ No. 61 is dated on the 334th day of 
the 2nd year of the reign of a king, who styles himself Tribhuvanachakravartin 
Kénérinmai-kogday. As I have shown in the introduction to No. 21 (page 110), this is 
not a proper name, but a title which is applied to various kings. The inscription records, 

‘that the king had built the shrine on which it is engraved, and which was called Ulagu- 
murudum-udaiya-Nachchiyar, z.e., “the goddess who owns the whole world,” within the 
Rajarajésvara temple at Taiijavar, and that he presented to that shrine eleven vél of 
land in the village of Kottagarkkudi, alias Ulag-Anda-nayaki-nallir. The second 
name, which means “the good village of the goddess who rules the world,” was evidently 
bestowed on the village with reference to the goddess, to whose shrine it was given. The four 
boundaries of the land which had been granted, were to be marked with stones, on which 
a trident, the emblem of Siva, was engraved? (paragraph 6).

I.—ADDITIONAL INSCRIPTIONS IN THE TANJAVUR TEMPLE. 


In the introductory remarks to No. 58 (page 229 f.) I had occasion to refer to four 
inscriptions of R&jardjadéva, the lower portions of which are buried underground. Two 
of these (Nos. 65 and 66),— which, to judge from their beginnings, promised a rich harvest 
of proper names,— were since temporarily excavated, and impressions of them taken, by my 
assistants. This led to the discovery of two further inscriptions, which are engraved under- 
neath No. 66, one of Rajéndradéva (No. 67), and one of Vikrama-Chéladéva (No. 68). I 
did not consider it worth while to excavate and copy the whole of Nos. 63 and 64, but shall 
now publish their first two lines as specimens. 


No. 63. ON THE OUTSIDE OF THE NORTH ENCLOSURE. 


From the published portion of No. 63, we learn that this inscription consists of a list 
of shepherds who had to suppiy ghee for temple lamps from the milk of a number of cattle, 
which had been presented to the temple before the 29th year of the reign of Rajarajadéva 
by the king himself and by others, or bought from the funds of the temple. To each lamp 
were allotted 96 ewes,) or 48 cows, or 16 she-buffaloes. The daily supply for each lamp was 
one urukku of ghee.

No. 65. ON THE OUTSIDE OF THE NORTH ENCLOSURE. 


This inscription records an order of king Rajar&éjadéva, by which he assigned a daily 
allowance of paddy to each of forty-eight persons, whom he had appointed before the 29th 
year of his reign, in order to recite the Tiruppadiyam in the temple, and to two persons who 
had to accompany the others on drums. This statement is of considerable importance for the 
history of Tamil literature’ as an unmistakable proof of the existence of the Saiva hymns 
which go by the name of padiyam or padiyam, and which are collected in the Dévéram, in 
the time of Rajardéja. The names of the fifty incumbents serve to corroborate this identi- 
fication of the Ziruppadiyam with the Dévdram, as part of them are derived from the names 
of the three authors of the Dévdram,' viz.. Tirundnasambandan (paragraph 7) or Sam- 
bandap (10, 22, 34, 38, 42), Tirunavukkaraiyay® (6, 12, 14, 19, 28, 43, 45), and 
Nambi-Arfiran (41, 44) or Arfran (19, 22), ‘The name of two other incumbents, 
Siralan (18, 15),” is derived from Siraladévar, one of the sixty-three Saiva devotees, who 
is referred to in No. 43, paragraph 19. A number of other names pre-supposes the exist- 
ence of certain Saiva temples which, without exception, are mentioned in the Periyapurd- 
nam. Among these are the temples at Tiruvafijiyam (2), Ar fr (8) or Sri-A rdir (21),

Tiruvaymér (30), Maraikkadu (41) or Tirumaraikka[du] (17), Aiy4ru (46), 
and perhaps Tiruvidaimarudar (51). The name Venkidan (16, 27, 29, 36, 40) is 
derived from Venkaédu or Tiruvenkadu, after which the mother of the saint Straladévar 
was called Tiruvenkattu-Nangai.' The god at Chidambaram is alluded to by the 
names Ambalavan (11), Ambalattadi (4, 47), Ambalakkiittay (18), Kattan (20, 26, 29, 31, 
49), Tillaikkfttan (49), Tillaikkaraigu (33), and Eduttapidam (9, 24, 32). 

The name Tiruven4val (3) is identical with diru-ven-ndval, “the sacred white jambd 
tree” in the Saiva temple on the island of Srirangam near Trichinopoly. This temple is 
now called JambukéSvara, Tiruv4paikka va]? or (by the Post Office) Tiruvinaikkéyil. 
The first of these three names means “(the image of) Igvara (ie. , Siva) (under) the jambd 
(tree),”? and the two others are corruptions of the ancient name of the locality, véz., Tiru- 
vanaikka, “the sacred elephant-grove.” The full designation of thé god, as used in the 
Jambuké$vara inscriptions, is “the lord of the sacred elephant-grove (Tiruvdnaikka), adias 
the lord of the three worlds, who is pleased to reside gladly under the shade of the sacred white 
jambé tree (tiru-ven-ndval).”” This name and the modern name JambukéSvara refer to an 
ancient legend, which is thus narrated in the Periyapurdnam (p. 239 of the Madras edition 
of 1888):— “In @ grove near the Chandratirtha (ie. the Moon-tank) in the Chéla 
country, a linga of Siva made its appearance under a white jumbd tree (ven-ndval). This was 
daily worshipped by a white elephant. Therefore the place received the name of “the sacred 
elephant-grove” (Tiruvanaikka). Over the linga, a spider constructed a canopy, in order 
to prevent dry leaves from dropping on the litga. When the elephant saw the cobwebs, he 
tore them down, because he considered them out of place. The spider became angry, crawled 
into the trunk of the elephant and bit it. The animal dashed its trunk on the ground and 
died. So did the spider. In due course, the spider was reborn as the son of the Chéla 
king Subhadéva and of his queen Kamalavati. The boy received the name K6- Sengan- 
ndn* and inherited his father’s kingdom. He possessed the faculty of remembering his 
former births and constructed a temple of Siva near the white jambdé tree in the sacred 
elephant-grove, where he, as a spider, had formerly worshipped the linga.” A distinct 
allusion to this legend occurs in a Jambukésvara inscription of the Pandya king Ké-Miara- 
varman, alias Kulasékharadéva, which mentions “ the sacred street called after (the god) 
who transformed a spider into a Chéla (king).”* That the legend, and the Jambukésvara 
temple itself, was in existence in about A.D. 1000, may be concluded from the subjoined 
inscription, in which the word tiruveln]ndval forms part of the name of one of the donees. 

Of historical interest is the name Réjadittan (47), which appears to have been be- 
stowed on its bearer in commemoration of Rajiditya, the Chéla contemporary of the 
Rashtrakdta king Krishna ITI.°

1. Hail ! Prosperity ! Until the twenty-ninth year (of the reign) of K6-Rajakésari- 
varman, alias Sri- Rajarajadéva, who, in his life of growing strength, during which, — 
(in) the belief that, as well as the goddess of fortune, the goddess of the great earth had 
become his wife,— he was pleased to destroy the ships (a?) Kandaldr-Salai, and conquered 
by his army, which was victorious in great battles, Véngai-nadu, Gateaniai. Tadigai- 
padi, Nulamba-padi, Kudamalai-nadu, Kollam, Kalingam, fra-mandalam, (which 
was the country) of the Singalas who possessed rough strength, the seven and a half lakshas 
of Iratta-pAdi, and twelve thousand ancient islands of the sea,— deprived the Seriyas of 
(their) splendour at the very moment when (they were) resplendent (fo such a degree) that

their company, and one person who should constantly beat the big drum (hotti-mattalam)®

daily allowance (nibandha) of three huruni of paddy each, (measured) by the marakkdl called

who would die or emigrate,* the nearest relations of such persons were to receive that paddy

No. 66. ON THE OUTSIDE OF THE NORTH ENCLOSURE. 


This very long inscription, which bears the same date as No. 65, and resembles it 
in style, records an order of king Rijarajadéva, by which he assigned the produce of 
certain land to a number of; men who had to perform various services in connection with the 
temple, and to four hundred women, evidently dancing-girls, who had been transferred to 
- the establishment of the Rajardjésvara temple from that of other temples in the Chéla 
country. Each person received one or more shares, each of which consisted of the produce 
of one véli of land, which was calculated at 100 kalam of paddy. This statement is valuable, 
as it enables us to ascertain, by a comparison of the produce in paddy with the extent 
of the land, that the unnamed land-measure, which is referred to in two other Tafijivar 
inscriptions of Rajaraja (Nos. 4 and 5), is meant for the véli. According to the Dictionnaire 
- Lamoul-Frangais, the modern equivalent of the véli is 26,755 square metres. 

Paragraphs 3 to 402 contain a list of the names of the dancing-girls whom Rajaraja 
had imported and settled in the neighbourhood of the Tafijavir temple. The names of 
_some of these women are of historical interest, as they refer to the designations of sacred 
places and of royal personages. Of the latter kind are:— Rajaraji (paragraphs 65 and 
268), Rajakésari (10), and Arumori® (236, 369), which are derived from different names 
of the reigning king, The name Kundavai (215) is identical with that of Rajaraja’s elder 
sister,® and the name Arifiji (400) appears to be connected with Arimjaya, the Sanskrit 
name of his grandfather? The name Seyya-Séram (280) may be connected with the 
-Chola king Sengan,® and the name Kannaradévi (244) reminds of king Kannaradéva, 
whom Mr. Venkayya has satisfactorily identified with the Rashtrakita king Krishna 
III. To the name of each woman is prefixed the name of the temple or village, to which 
she had been attached before her final transfer to the Rajarajésvara temple. On the basis 
-of these references, and of the names of part of the women themselves, which allude to 
temples and villages, we can draw up a list of temples which were already in existence

A few of the women are called after Vaishnava shrines which are mentioned in 
the Néldyiraprabundham, viz., Arangam (Srirangam), Tiruvéngadam (Tirumalai), Ali 
(Tiruvali), and Sikurugtr (Tirukkurugir). Others were transferred to Tafijavar from 
temples which, to judge from the second part of their names,’ belong to the Vaishnava sect, 
viz, Avanindrayana-Vinnagar at Ambar, Sritari-Vinnagar.at Arapuram, and 
Sripfidi-Vinnagar at Pambuni. 

The second part of the inscription (paragraphs 403 to 510) consists of a list of male 
temple servants, vz., dancing-masters, musicians, drummers, singers, accountants, parasol. 
bearers, lamp-lighters, watermen, potters, washermen, barbers, astrologers, tailors, a brazier, 
carpenters, a goldsmith, and others the reading or meaning of whose designations remains 
doubtful. Some of these persons are called after king Rajara ja (paragraphs 424, 425, 447, 
466, 493, 494, 496, 498, 503) and after his surnames Arumori (406, 466), Mummadi- 
Chéla® (403, 404, 423, 436, 455, 465, 486), Nityavinédda* (418, 504), Rajakésarin 
(467), and Rajaéraya® (413); others after his father Pardntaka (448, 458, 496) and 
after his grandfather Arimjaya (416, 507, 509). Thetwo names Kandardaditta (508) 
and Madurantaka (504) probably refer to the two Chila kings Gandardaditya and 
Madhurantaka.® The name Taila (435) reminds of the Western Chalukya king Taila IT.

TRANSLATION. 

1, Tail! Prosperity ! Until the twenty-ninth year (of the reign) of K6-Rajakésarivar- 
man, alias Sri-Rajarajadéva, who, ete." — the lord Sri-Rajarajadéva had (1) given 
(a number of) Nivandakkarar* as Nivandakkdrar of the lord of the Sri-Rajaraj @Svara(temple), 
and (2) transferred (4 number of) temple women ® from (other) temple establishments‘ of the 
Chéla country (Séra-mandalam) as temple women of the lord of the Sri-Rajarajésvara 
(temple). To (these persons) shares (pangu) were allotted as allowance (nibandha). (The value) 
of each share (which consisted of the produce) of (one) vélc of land, was to be one hundred kalam 
of paddy, (measured) by the marakkdl called (after) Adawallan, which is equal to a rdjakésari. 
Instead of those among these sharcholders, who would die or emigrate, the nearest relations 
of such persons were to receive that allowance (Adn7) and to do the work. If the nearest 
relations were not qualified themselves, (they) were to select (other) qualified persons, to let 
(these) do the work, and to receive (the allowance). If there were no near relations, the (other) 
incumbents of such appointments‘ were to select qualified persons from those fit for such 
appointments, and the person selected was to receive the allowance. Accordingly, (the names 
of these persons) were engraved on stone, as the lord Sri-Rajarajadévahad been pleased 
to order. 

2. The temple women (were the following) :— 

3. To [S]é[ra]man[gai}, a girl (who has been transferred from the establishment of the 
temple) of Lokamahadévi-{évara at Tiruvaiyaru,’ (and who resides in) the first house 
of the southern row (sragu) of the temple street on the south (of the temple), one share. 


* The historical part of this inscription is identical with that of No. 65.

stipendiaries.’ 

5 The literal meaning of saflé@ eAdQuew@sar is :— “women (who reside) in the streets near the 
temple,” which are occupied by the temple servants.

° paaer probably stands for sa@ tw (Sanskrit nagné), as gdiner and géaar for sic and game; 
see page 8, note 4. 

7 According to Mr. Venkayya’s account in the Madras Christian College Magazine for May 1891, a small 
shrine, which is now called Uttara-Kailisa, in the Pafichanadisvara temple at Tiruvaiyéru (see p. 258, note 4), 
bears several inscriptions of Rajaraja and Rajéndra-Chéla, which record that this shrine was built by Tandi- 
éattividahgiyar (i.e., Dantiéakti-Vitanki), alias Lékamahadévi, a queen of Rajarajadéva, and that it was 
therefore called LokamahAdéyi-Iévara. his is evidently the shrine to which paragraph 3 refers.

No. 67. ON THE OUTSIDE OF THE NORTH, ENCLOSURE. 


This inscription is dated in the 6th year of the reign of K6-Parakésarivayman, alias 
Rajéndradéva, aud opens with a short poetical account of the deeds of this king, from 
which we lcarn that he invaded Irattap4di, ze, the Western Chalukya empire, and that 
he defeated Ahavamalla at Koppam on the bank of the “ great river.” As I have stated 
in the introductory remarks of the Tafijavar inscription of Kuléttunga (ante, page 232), the 
battle of Koppam or Koppai is referred to in the Kaliigattu-Parani (viii. 27),” and a Koppam

The immediate object of the Tafijavar inscription of Rajéndradéva is to record that, in 
the 4th year of his reign, the king assigned a daily allowance of paddy to a troop of actors 
who had to perform a drama, entitled Rijardjésvara-ndtaka, in the RajarajéSvara temple 
on the occasion of an arfnual festival in the month of Vaigisi. Two_years later, in the, 6th 
year of his reign, the king further ordered that his previous donation should be engraved 

_ou the stone wall of the temple. 

I cannot say if manuscripts of the Rdjardjésvara-ndtaka still exist; but it may be safely 
roncluded from the wording of the title that the subject of this drama was the foundation of 
the Tafijavar temple by the great Rajarija. It also follows from the mention of the 
term Rajarajésvara in an inscription of Rajéndradéva that this king belonged to a later period 
than that of Rajaraja and, consequently, of the latter’s son and successor Rajéndra-Chila. 
Though this posteriority of Rajéndradéva is already evident from the more recent form of the 
alphabet of his inscriptions and from certain synchronisms between, the Chélas and Chalu- 
kyas,? I consider it necessary to draw attention to the direct proof afforded by the present 
instription, because Mr. Kanakasabhai has lately expressed the opinion that both Rajaraja 
and Ltajéndra-Chdla were among the successors of Parakésarivarman, alias Rajéudradéva.$

malla) proceeded to Koppam on the bank of the great river and fought against (Aim). (But 
he) converted into reeking corpses (that) covered the earth, the whole warlike army of 
Ahavamalla. Having perceived this, Ahavamalla became afraid, incurred disgrace, and 
ran away. (‘'te king) seized his elephants and horses, troops of camels, women and treasures, 
and anointed himself (c commemoration) of the victory. Tn the sixth year ( (of the reign) of 
(this) K 6-Parakésarivarman, alas the lord Sri- Rajéndrad éva, who was E geacoualy 
seated on the throne of heroes.

No. 68. ON THE OUTSIDE OF THE NORTH ENCLOSURE. 

This inscription is dated in the 4th year of the reign of K6-Parakésarivarman, 
akas Vikrama-Chéladéva, and records that the king assigned an allowance to a person 
who measured the paddy in the R&jarajéSvara temple and in the villages belonging to it. 
This man was evidently a controlling officer who had to check the supplies of paddy, which, 
according to many of the inscriptions published in this volume, had to be delivered into the 
temple stores.

The order of the king is preceded by a poetical account of his decds. Though this’ 
passage is, on the whole, of a purely panegyrical character, it contains a few statements 
which appear to be based on historical facts. While still a youth, — probably. only heir- 
apparent, — Vikrama-Chila is said to have put to flight the Telinga Bhima of Kulam, to 
have burnt the Kalinga country, and to have stayed in the Véngai-mandalam, z.e., the 
Véngi country. In my Annual Report for 1893-94, page 6, I have noticed some inscrip- 
tions of the chiefs of Kamalikarapura or (in Telugu) Kolanu, which is probably the 
modern Ellore! on the bank of the Kolleru lake in the Gddavari district. The earliest 
known member of this family is Katama-Nayaka, who is mentioned in two inscriptions of+ 
Saka 1062 and 1070 at Drakshardma (Nos. 204 and 347 of 1893). The same chief is the 
donor of a copper-plate grant of Saka 1056, which has been published by’ Dr. Fleet.? He is 
there stated to have been the lord of Sarasipuri or K olanu’ on the bank of a great lake 
(viz., the Kolleru lake) in the Véngi-mandala and to have been a vassal of Kuléttunga 
II. As the Tafijavdr inscription of Vikrama-Chéla connects the Véngai-mandalam with 
Kulam, whose lord Bhima was put to flight by the king, and as the Tamil word su/am, ‘a 
tank,’ is etymologically identical with the Telugu Zolanu, ‘a lake,’ it may be safely con- 
cluded that the Teliiga Bhima of the Tafijavdr inscription belonged to the same dynasty as 
Katama-Nayaka of Kolanu. 

« After his stay in the Véngai-mandalam, the subjoined inscription informs us, Vikrama. 
Chéla went to the South and: claimed the crown of the country on the banks of the Kavért, 
ae, the Chola country. The passage which conveys this information, is also met with in. 
the inscriptions of Kuléttunga I.* As none of the predecessors of Kuldttunga I. bore the 
name Vikrama-Chéla, it is clear that the passage in question was taken over by the composer 
of Vikrama-Chéla’s inscriptions from those of Kuléttunga I., and that, in trying to identify 
the Vikrama-Chéla of the present inscription, we must look fer him among the successors of 
Kuldttunga I. The only Vikrama-Chéla who is known from other sources but the subjoined 
inscription, vz., from a copper-plate grant® and from a Tamil chronicle,*® was the immediate 
successor of Kuldttunga I, I have no hesitation in identifying this Vikrama-Chéla, who 
reigned from Saka 1034 to 1049,’ with the king°of the same name to whose reign the 
Tafijivdr inscription belongs., A confirmation of, the identity of both may be derived from 
verse 24 of the third inscription * on the Pithapuram pillar :—

“When he (vz, Vikrama-Chéda), whose other name was Tydgasamudra, had 
gone to protect the Chéda-mandala, the Véngi country became devoid of a ruler in 
that interval.” 

Here we have an independent variant of the statement, made in the Tafijavdr inscrip- 
tion, that Vikrama-Chéla originally resided in Véigt and that he left it to ascend the Chéla 
throne. Another point of agreement is still more decisive: Mr. Venkayya informs me that, 
in his copy of the Tanjore MS. of the Vikkirama-Séran-Uld, the surname Tyagasamudra 
is twice applied to Vikrama-Chéla.’ 

Finally the Tafijavar inscription acquaints us with the names of two queens, Muk- 
kékkirdnadi and Tyagapatéka. The former, whom the poet compares to the goddess 
Parvati, was evidently Vikrama-Chéla’s chief queen, and the second, who is compared to 
Ganga, his favourite. 

The text of the historical introduction has been compared with that of two similar 
inscriptions of Vikrama-Chéla, one of the 5th year of his reign in the Tydgaréja temple 
at Tiruvariir in the Negapatam talluga (No. 164 of 1894) and another of the 11th year in 
the Apatsahay éévara temple? at Alangudi in the Kumbhakdnam talluga (No. 165 of 1894), 
Other inscriptions of Vikrama;Chéla open with a much shorter historical introduction, the 
first words of which are yore vers, viz. one of the 9th year in the Arulala-Perumal 
temple at Tiruvattiy dr or Little Conjeeveram (No. 33 of 1893), one of the same year and 
one of the 14th year at Pallavaram in the Chingleput talluga. These inscriptions mention 
the burning, or conquest, of the Kalinga country® and the name of one of Vikrama- 
Chéla’s queens, vz., Mukkékkirdnadi, and must, accordingly, belong to the time of the 
same king as the other set, the introductions of which open with the words yurda Honég. 

Thanks to the calculations of Mr. 8, B. Dikshit and Professor Kielhorn, I am able to 
state the probable day of the accession of Vikrama-Chéla. ‘The third line of the 
Tiruvardr inscription to which reference was made in the preceding paragraph, contains 
the following date :—

* TRANSLATION. 


1. Hail! Prosperity! (The king) was resplendent with golden chains, combined with 
garlands of flowers. In (fds) arms, which were covered with large jewels, (and) which (formed 
the subject of) a great number of poems, rested the goddess of Victory, along with the goddess 
of the great Earth, Having obtained as her own (possession) (is) breast, (which was) her 
support, the goddess of Prosperity exclusively abided (there). As a chaste woman that 
possessed great eloquence, the goddess of Learning resided with delight in (A¢s) tongue. (His) 
sceptre, along with the wheel (of his authority), swayed over all regions. (His) white parasol 
was raised on high, like a matchless second moon, overspreading the whole world. The 
dark Kali (age) hid itself and lay in the deep pit. , 

At the time of love’ (i.e, in his youth), (he) grasped the cruel weapon, so that the 
Telinga Viman (ze, Bhima) of Kulam® ascended the mountains (as refuge), and so 
that intense fire consumed the country (bhdim?) of Kalinga. (He) joyfully stayed (awhile) 
in the Véngai-mandalam and put on the garland of (the victory over) the Northern region. 

(Ze) stopped the prostitution of the goddess with the sweet and excellent lotus-flower 
(i.e., Lakshmi) of the Southern region, and the loneliness of the goddess of the good country 
whose garment is the Popni (Kavéri), and put on by right (of inheritance) the pure royal 
crown of jewels. 

While (he) diffused his kindness, (?¢) spread to every individual. The whole earth 
rejoiced; the tongue of the bell* became silent ; (As) victory and fame rose higher and 
higher. 
The Seriyas (.¢., Pandyas) entered hot jungles (as refuge); the Seralas (te, Chéras) 
entered the sea; the Singalas (i.e. Sitmhalas), who deal destruction, became afraid and 
agitated in mind; the Gangas paid tribute; the Kanuadas turned (ther) backs; the 
Kongas retreated ; the Konkanas fied; the kings of all other regions duly worshipped 
(fus) red lotus-feet as their protection. 

Mukkékkirdnadi, the jewel among the inhabitants of the forest-country, * who was 
born to be worshipped by the seven ancient worlds, joyfully dwelt in harmony (with him), 
just as Sarnkara dwells with Uma on the Imaiyam (¢.¢., Himilaya).

No. 69.—On THE OUTSIDE OF THE EAST ENCLOSURE. 


This inscription and the next following one (No. 70) are engraved on the right of the 
entrance to the second gépura.4 The inscription No. 69 consists of a list of villages which 
had to supply treasurers, servants and accountants to the RajarajéSvara temple, in accord- 
ance with an order which RAjardjadéva had issued before the 29th year of his reign. 
Paragraph 1 states that these villages were situated in the Chéla country, in the Pandya 
country, and in Tondai-nddu which was surnamed Jayankonda-Chéla-mandalam. 
Tondai-nadu or Tondai-mandalam is the ancient Tamil name of the Pallava country.® 
In Sanskrit inscriptions it occurs as Tondtra-mandala, Tundira-mandala, and 
Tundaka-vishaya.® The present inscription proves that Jayankonda-Chéla-manda- 
lam, which is referred to in many inscriptions,’ is another name of Tondai-mandalam. 
Jayankonda-Chéla, from which this term is derived, must have been a surname of 
Rajaraja or of one of his predecessors. In the Madras Christian College Magazine for October 
1890, Mr. Venkayya has shown that proper names, of which Jayankonda-Chéla forms the 
first member, do not occur in inscriptions previous to the 29th, year of Rajardja’s reign, 
and concludes from this fact that Jayankonda-Chéla was a surname of Rajaraja himself, 
assumed by him towards the close of his reign. The same surname was subsequently

TRANSLATION. 

1. Hail! Prosperity ! Before the twenty-ninth year (of the reign) of K6-Rajakésari- 
varman, alias Sri-Rajarajadéva, who, &c.,2 — the lord Sri-Rajarajadéva was pleased 
to order that the inhabitants of the brahmadéyas in Sdra-mandalam, in Pandi-nadu, 
atas Rajaraja-mandalam,’ and in Tondai-nadu, alias Jayankonda-Séra-mandalam, 
should supply, as long as the moon and the sun endure, to the lord of the Sri-Raj ja- 
rajéSvara (temple) : (1) as temple treasurers, such Braéhmamas in those respective brahmadéyas 
as are rich in land, connexions, or capital; (2) Brahmacharins (mért) as temple servants ; 
and (3) accountants for writing the accounts (of the temple). Among the persons who are sup- 
plied, to each treasurer should be measured. . . .,. - + + ~ « hulam of paddy per 
year ; to each Brahmacharin who is a temple servant, (one) padakhu of paddy per day and four 
kiSu per year ; among these, to each of ten who had taken permanent vows (?), three duruné 
of paddy per day and four Ad§u per year ; among the sama, to each of twenty . . . . . 

+ «+ « «4 (one) padakku of paddy per day and five kdsu per year; to each person who 
writes the accounts, two hundred kalam of paddy per year; to each under-accountaat whom 
the latter has to supply, seventy-five kalam of paddy per year, ze, one hundred and fifty 
kalam of paddy to two (under-accountanis), Among these, the Brahmachdrins who are 
temple servants, shall receive (their) allowance of paddy and idSu at the city treasury of the 
lord of the Sri-RajarajéSvara (¢emple); and the treasurers and accountants shall receive 
(their allowances) at the up-country treasuries of the lord of the Sri-Rajarajéévara (temple), 
These allowances were engraved on stone by order of the lord Sri-Rajardjadéva. 

2. The members of the assembly of Ma[agat]jam in Mangala-nadu, (a subdimsion) 
of Arumoridéva-valanddu, have to supply one Brahmana as temple treasurer (and) one 
Brahmacharin as temple servant. 

3. The members of the assembly of Nedumanal, alias Madanamafijari-chaturvé- 
dimangalam, in Nenmali-nddu, (a subdivision) of Arumoridéva-valanadu, have to 
supply two Brahmacharins as temple servants. 

4, The members of the assembly of Kunriydr in the same ndédu have to supply one 
Brahmachirin as temple servant.

No. 70. ON THE OUTSIDE OF THE EAST ENCLOSURE. 


This inscription consists of a list of villages in the Chéla country, which had to supply 
watchmen for the temple, in accordance with an order which Rajarajadéva had issued 
before the 29th year of his reign. The last paragraph (114) states that, owing to want of 
space, the inscription is continued on the south of “the gate of Rajar4aja,” z.c., on the left 
of the entrance to the second gépura. This missing portion is identical with the inscription 
No. 57, which professes to be the continuation of an incomplete inscription on the north of 
“the gate of Rajaraja,” ¢.e., on the right of the entrance to the seeond gépura.

No. 70. INSCRIPTION OF RAJARAJA. 333 


TRANSLATION. 


1. [Hail! Prosperity! ] Before the twenty-ninth year (of the reign) of Ké-Rajaké. 
sarivarman, alias Sri-Rajarajadéva, who, &c.,W— the lord Sri-Rajarajadéva [was 
pleased to order that the inhabitants of the] brahma[déyas] in SOra-mandalam [should 
supply temple watchmen] to the lord of the Sri-Rajarajé4vara (temple).2 To each of the 
temple watchmen who are supplied, the inhabitants of the respective villages which have 
supplied the temple watchmen, shall measure one hundred dalam of paddy per year. This 
paddy has to be supplied and daily allowances (padi) have to be paid every year, as long 
as the moon and the sun endure, out of the tax due by the inhabitants of the respective 
villages. These allowances were engraved on stone by order of the lord Sri-Rajaraja- 
déva.
